prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Two floors up, at the corner of Hearst and Shattuck, he’s clamped for good in an iron lung. When it’s time to eat he nudges his head a sweaty mile to the edge of the pillow. It takes a while. His brilliant bloodshot light-blue eyes steer me from cupboard to fridge: he would like his chicken burrito cut into bite-size pieces, a bent straw for his glass of water, please. How does the body live its only life in a cage? I watch him compute the distance from bar to bar, and squeeze between them with a violent compression, a fury of bursting free that doesn’t last. His will is a crowbar, angled to pry up the rooted intractable weight of matter. I watch him slyly, I check out the way he does it. He does it. But pain in its absolute privacy weighs what it weighs. I come here to study the soul, posing one question a dozen ways, most of them silent. “If I’m only a body,” he laughs, “I’m up shit creek.” His laugh a gritty eruption of rock, salt and breath. Like me he writes poems but he does it letter by letter on a propped keyboard, the mouth-stick wobbling between his teeth. That kind of speed keeps a poet accountable. He won’t ever say, “The grass is very green” when it’s only green.

Enclosed within the metallic chamber of an iron lung, a man’s entire physical existence is governed by a rhythmic, mechanical breath. Bound by total paralysis, he relies completely on the steady hands of caregivers for the most fundamental acts of survival—a simple sip of water, a bite of food, or the subtle adjustment of his head. As I observe him day after day, my aim is to look beyond the clinical realities of his care. I watch him closely to conduct a quiet study of the human soul, seeking to understand how profound physical suffering can exist alongside an undiminished spirit.

To live in such severe confinement is to endure a constant, quiet agony, yet beneath his immobile exterior burns a fierce and unyielding determination to transcend the limits of his flesh. Remarkably, he does not allow his world to shrink to the dimensions of a steel cylinder. Instead, he meets his harsh reality with a surprising, buoyant sense of humor. By laughing at the absurdities of his condition, he asserts a crucial truth: his true identity is not defined by his damaged body. He firmly believes that who he is—his mind, his spirit, his essence—exists entirely outside the physical vessel that houses him.

This transcendental philosophy finds its most vivid expression in his creative life. Using a stick held delicately between his teeth, he writes poetry letter by agonizing letter. It is a painstaking process that demands extraordinary patience and physical exertion. Yet, this very limitation transforms his art. Because every single keystroke costs him so much effort, there is no room for waste, vanity, or deceit in his work. The agony of creation forces an absolute precision, compelling him to select only the most vital words and stripping his poetry down to a rare, luminous honesty.

Through his endurance, humor, and art, he offers a profound lesson in resilience. He demonstrates that while the physical body may be deeply compromised and confined, the human spirit possesses an infinite capacity to overcome its circumstances, turning even the weightiest suffering into enduring grace.

The room was defined by a single, relentless rhythm: the deep, mechanical sigh of the iron lung. It was a sound that filled the small space, a rhythmic hiss and thud that dictated the very cadence of life inside it. I had come searching for an answer to an ancient, harrowing question: when the physical body is reduced to a stillness so total it resembles a tomb, what becomes of the human spirit? 

Inside the polished steel cylinder lay a man whose world had shrunk to the diameter of his own neck. Paralyzed from the collarbone down, his existence was mediated entirely through mirrors, medical apparatuses, and the artificial breathing forced upon his lungs by the bellows of the machine. Yet, suspended above his face was a resting canvas, and between his teeth he held a long, lightweight wooden rod tipped with a soft rubber point. 

I watched him write. 

The process was agonizingly deliberate. To form a single word, he had to tilt his head, align the stick with an overhead keyboard apparatus, and press down with precise, trembling pressure. *Tap. Pause. Tap. Pause.* A single line of verse did not take minutes; it took hours. A complete stanza was an ordeal of days, requiring immense physical stamina from muscles he could barely control, synchronized perfectly with the machine’s involuntary intake of air.

As I sat in the dim corner of the room, observing this quiet struggle, a profound realization began to take shape. For those of us with functioning limbs, language is cheap. We spill words onto paper in careless torrents, relying on speed and ease, often filling space with trivialities because the physical act of writing costs us nothing. 

For this poet, however, every letter was bought with sweat, pain, and exhausting concentration. 

This extreme constraint eliminated all room for vanity or fluff. Because a single misplaced adjective would demand ten minutes of grueling physical labor to erase and correct, every word had to justify its own existence. The mouth-stick forced upon him an absolute economy of language, an unprecedented artistic accountability. His condition stripped away the frivolous, leaving behind only the most vital, crystalline truths. He could not afford a lazy metaphor; he could not waste a breath.

In that sterile room, amidst the odor of antiseptic and the monotonous hum of the respirator, I realized I was not witnessing a tragedy of imprisonment, but a triumph of liberation. The steel hull of the iron lung bound his flesh, but it could not touch his imagination. Through the narrow conduit of a wooden stick held between his teeth, he was building universes, questioning fate, and articulating the subtle beauty of a world he could only glimpse in a mirror.

His willpower had converted a devastating physical limitation into a crucible for pure, uncompromising art. In the deliberate, letter-by-letter creation of his poetry, he proved that while the body may be trapped in the deepest dark, the human soul possesses an unyielding, luminous capacity to transcend its cage.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poignant vignette about visiting a poet who lives in an iron lung.
counterfactuals.output:
The room breathed in a slow, mechanical three-four time. 

*Hiss-drag-click.* 

It was the cadence of a heavy iron tide, pulling air into Julian’s static lungs and sweeping it out again. In the center of the room sat the machine: a yellowing cylinder of painted steel, ribbed with rubber seals and brass rivets, resembling a forgotten bathysphere anchored in a sea of dusty books.

Only his head emerged from the neck collar, resting on a flat, white pillow. Above him, a small angled mirror flickered with the reflection of the window—a square of pale October sky and the dark, tangled fingers of an oak tree.

“You brought… the rain,” Julian said. 

His voice was a rasp, thin as parchment, carefully metered to match the machine’s rhythm. He could only speak on the exhale, when the bellows pushed the air back out of his chest, forcing sound past his quiet vocal cords.

“Just a drizzle,” I said, stepping closer. I set a damp coat over the back of a wooden chair. “The leaves are turning.”

I reached into my pocket and pulled out a single maple leaf, brilliant and wet, stained the color of a fresh bruise. I held it up, not to his face, but to the mirror above his eyes so he could see it.

Julian’s eyes—bright, piercingly clear, and vast enough to hold a navy—fixed on the reflection. The blue-gray iris widened slightly. The machine *hissed*, forcing a breath into him, holding him captive in its artificial swell. 

Then came the *click*, the release. 

“A crimson… sail,” he whispered on the sigh of air. “Sinking… in the gutter.”

I smiled, pulling out a small leather journal and a pen. I was his hands, his paper, his witness. “Is that the start of one?”

“Page… forty,” he murmured, waiting for the next mechanical gulp. The bellows contracted. *Hiss.* The negative pressure vacuumed the air into his chest, expanding a ribs cage that had forgotten how to move on its own forty years ago. 

*Click.* 

“Write this,” he rasped on the falling tide. 

*“The iron knows… no season.* 
*It wears… no autumn coat.* 
*Yet here… upon the glass…* 
*A hundred red trees… float.”*

I wrote the words down, the scratching of my nib on paper playing counterpoint to the steady, rhythmic thrum of the pump. 

When I finished, I lowered the leaf and sat beside him. The room smelled of lavender, stale tea, and ozone—the faint, metallic tang of electricity that kept him tethered to the living. 

“Is it terrifying?” I asked softly. It was a question I had wanted to ask for months, one that felt too heavy, yet the silence between us made room for it. “Living inside the breath of something else?”

Julian’s eyes shifted from the mirror down to mine, as far as his neck would allow. The bellows pulled. *Hiss.* His chest rose beneath the steel shell, invisible to me, but felt in the shift of the room's air.

*Click.*

“We are all… inside it,” he whispered, the words riding his mechanical exhale like leaves on a slow river. “You just… hear yours… coming.”

He closed his eyes, his face settling into a profound, terrifying peace. The machine kept breathing for him, a faithful, galvanized beast, counting down the seconds in a song made entirely of rust and air. I picked up my pen, waited for the next exhale, and stayed to write it down.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a literary descriptive excerpt set in Berkeley about visiting a disabled fellow writer confined to a medical device. Focus on themes of physical limitation versus mental freedom, the precision of language, and the weight of existence.
counterfactuals.output:
The late-afternoon sun over the Berkeley hills did not warm; it merely gilded the edges of things, turning the peeling brown shingles of the old Craftsman home into plates of rusted armor. Outside, the air smelled of salt from the Bay and the dry, medicinal sharpness of sun-baked eucalyptus. Inside, the world contracted to the diameter of a twelve-foot room, smelling faintly of rubbed isopropyl, stale Earl Grey, and the warm, mechanical ozone of a brass-and-steel pulmonary envelope.

Julian lay encased within the machine—a heavy, vintage iron lung modified with modern acrylic ports and micro-monitors, hummed into life by a piston that measured time not in seconds, but in atmospheres. It was a terrifyingly solid thing, an anchor of cast metal and ironclad seals that locked his fragile, ruined body to the floorboards. To look at him was to witness gravity magnified tenfold: his limbs were mere whispers beneath a linen sheet, his collarbones like dry driftwood cast upon a white shore.

And yet, his eyes—pale green, framed by the dark hollows of his skull—moved with a terrifying, unencumbered speed.

"You’re late," he said. The words did not flow; they were released in disciplined bursts, metered precisely to the machine’s rhythmic, exhaling sigh. *Hiss. Clack. Silence.*

When breath is rationed by a mechanical pulse, syntax loses its excess fat. Adjectives become expensive luxuries; adverbs, an unpardonable waste of oxygen. Julian had mastered a dialect of pure distillation. Over the hours, as the fog began its slow, ghostly crawl across the Golden Gate, obscuring the distant lights of San Francisco, I listened to him construct sentences that possessed the structural integrity of diamond. Where I stumbled through the clumsy, slouching prose of the fully able, Julian deployed nouns like scalpels.

"The manuscript," he murmured, his throat clicking on the *p*. "Chapter four. Too... ornamental. Strike... the metaphor."

"It sets the mood, Julian," I offered, sitting on the low wooden stool beside his steel shell.

His gaze shifted, pinning me to the chair with the sheer, weightless force of his intellect. "Mood... is a crutch. Give me... the physics of the grief. Not... the weather."

It was a profound perversion of nature, this room. His body was an absolute prisoner, bound to a drum of cold pressure that forced his ribcage to rise and fall in a manufactured choreography. The weight of his physical existence—the unbearable, agonizing mass of flesh that had failed him—was absolute. Yet, suspended in that iron cradle, Julian’s mind operated with an exhilarating, dangerous freedom. Stripped of the distractions of movement, unburdened by the mundane athletics of standing, walking, or reaching, his consciousness had expanded to fill the void. He was an astronomer trapped at the bottom of a well, staring up at a sky no one else could see, mapping constellations with absolute, unshakeable clarity.

The machine sighed again, a deep, synthetic lung-full of Bay air, pushed through rubber tubes into a man who lived entirely in the conditional tense.

He closed his eyes for a moment, resting between cycles. In the dimming light, the room felt less like a sickchamber and more like an observatory. 

"Read it back," he commanded softly on the next artificial exhale. "Without... the grace notes."

I took up the paper, holding it where he could see, and began to read. Under his silent, merciless tutelage, the clutter of my words dissolved, leaving only what was essential, heavy, and true.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a prose reflection exploring the question "What happens to the soul when the body is trapped?" centered on a character who types poetry using a mouth-stick keyboard.
counterfactuals.output:
The rubber tip tastes perpetually of cold silicone and stale tea. It sits between my molars, an eight-inch rod of lightweight aluminum extending from the center of my speechlessness like a rigid, single-feathered wing. 

People often ask—or rather, their eyes ask, hovering over the quiet rise and fall of my chest—what happens to the soul when the body turns to stone. They assume it shrinks. They imagine it curling into a bruised ball behind the ribs, suffocated by the heavy, indifferent flesh that refuses to obey it. They think of the trapped soul as a bird in a darkened cage, beating its wings into a quiet, exhausted coma.

They are wrong. 

When the body is trapped, the soul does not diminish; it pressurizes. 

Without hands to gesture, without legs to pace away anxiety, without the mundane squandering of kinetic energy that defines a walking life, the spirit has nowhere to dissipate. It cannot leak out through the fingertips or scatter itself across a room. Instead, it turns inward, compressing under the sheer weight of physical stillness. It becomes dense. It gathers at the back of the throat, hot and heavy as quicksilver, waiting for a single point of exit.

My point of exit is a twenty-six-letter grid glowing eighteen inches from my nose.

I dip my chin. The muscles in my neck—the only soldiers left in my command—tighten with a familiar, burning precision. The aluminum wand sways, then lands. 

*Clack.* 

The letter *B* blinks into existence on the blank digital page. 

It takes four seconds to steady my breath, adjust the angle of my head, and drive the stick downward again. 

*Clack.* 

*L.*

In my previous life, when my limbs moved like unthinking water, I was verbose. I wasted thousands of words a day on trivialities, letting thoughts spill out of me unrefined, scattering my inner life across the noisy floor of the world. But here, in the quiet architecture of paralysis, every word is an act of manual labor. Every stanza costs three hundred small, deliberate nods of the head. A single poem is a marathon run entirely within the column of my neck.

Because the tax on expression is so high, the soul learns a furious economy. It discards the frivolous. It strips away the adjectives, the polite evasions, the comfortable filler of human conversation. What is left is pure, concentrated essence. 

*Clack.* 

*O.*

If the body is a cage, the mouth-stick is not a key; it is a chisel. I am not trying to unlock the prison; I am carving my way through the walls, one micro-stroke at a time. 

I watch the cursor pulse, a steady, green heartbeat waiting for my next tilt of the head. In this light, the question of where the soul goes reveals its answer. It travels down the length of the metal rod. It leaves the damp warmth of my mouth, glides along the cold aluminum, and bursts out through the hard rubber tip onto the screen. 

For eight hours a day, my soul lives outside my skin. It resides in the white space between the lines. It dances in the cadence of a trochee, strides boldly across a line break, and leaps over the wide ocean of the margin—things my legs have not done for a decade.

*Clack.*

*O.*

When the body is trapped, the soul learns the geography of the absolute. It suffers, yes—it burns with the terrible agony of an engine idling at maximum speed while the wheels are locked in mud. But if it does not break under that pressure, it undergoes a metamorphosis. It turns from steam into liquid, from liquid into crystal. 

*Clack.*

*D.*

*Blood.* The word sits on the monitor, glowing, alive, born from the stillness.

I rest my chin against my chest, breathing through the nose, letting the burning ache in my shoulders subside. My body is anchored here, heavy and mute, tethered to gravity by dead weight. But as I align the stick for the next letter, I know the truth of this quiet room: 

The cage is made of bone and marrow. But the bird has learned to peck its way into eternity.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a scene for a memoir about visiting an inspiring friend who uses an iron lung. Include sensory details about helping him eat, his dark sense of humor, and his intense dedication to writing.
counterfactuals.output:
The air in Arthur’s room always carried a strange, dual climate: the top half smelled of old paper, pipe tobacco, and peppermint, while the bottom half smelled faintly of machine oil, warmed grease, and antiseptic. 

Dominating the center of the room was the cylinder—a massive, yellow-painted Emerson respirator that looked like a deep-sea submersible from a bygone century. Inside it lay Arthur. Only his head emerged, framed by a tight rubber collar that gripped his neck like a steady hand.

*Whoosh-click. Hiss-puff.*

The machine breathed for him, a rhythmic, iron tide pulling air into his lungs and pushing it back out. Eighteen breaths a minute. 

"Ah, the biographer arrives," Arthur said, his voice coming out in synchronized, clipped cadence with the exhaust valve. "Don’t stand too close to the intake, Leo. If the power cuts, you’ll have to blow into the pipe like a brass trumpet to keep me going."

I smiled, pulling up a wooden chair. "Good to see you too, Arthur."

"Look at me," he grunted, his dark eyes sparkling in the angled mirror suspended above his face. "Peak physical condition. I haven't lost an argument or a race in thirty years. Mostly because nobody has the heart to beat a man in a hot dog casing."

He laughed—a quick, dry cough that bumped against the machine's cadence. Arthur had contracted polio in 1952, at twenty-one. The world had moved on to microchips and space stations, but Arthur remained housed in two hundred pounds of steel. Yet, I had never met anyone who occupied more psychological space. 

"I brought the stew," I said, setting a heavy ceramic thermos and a towel on his bedside table. 

"Thank God. The nurse tried to feed me pureed carrots at noon. Tasted like wet cardboard and sadness."

Feeding Arthur was a ritual of absolute synchronicity. I draped the towel under his chin, uncovering the small patch of pale skin above the rubber gasket. Opening the thermos, the rich, fragrant steam of braised beef, rosemary, and garlic filled the room, instantly drowning out the smell of motor oil.

"All right," Arthur instructed, his eyes fixing on the spoon. "Remember the rhythm. If you shove it in while the chest expands, I’ll choke, die, and haunt your typewriter."

I ladled a small bite—a tender piece of beef bathed in thick gravy—and waited. 

*Whoosh.* The bellows expanded, pulling his chest outward. Inhale. 
*Click-hiss.* The pressure released. Exhale. 

"Now," Arthur whispered.

I slipped the spoon past his lips. He chewed deliberately, his throat straining as he swallowed just as the machine pulled the next breath. A tiny bead of gravy caught at the corner of his mouth. I wiped it away with the cloth, feeling the intense, radiant heat radiating from his face. It was shocking how warm he was, how fiercely alive, when everything below his jaw was encased in static iron.

"Sensational," he murmured, closing his eyes for a second. "More garlic than last time. Good. Keeps the vampires and the priests away."

Between mouthfuls, his eyes kept darting toward the rigged boom arm above his head. Clamped to it was a custom-built mouth-stick—a long plastic wand with a rubber tip—pointing toward an angled mechanical typewriter mounted on a tray. Pages of crisp bond paper were stacked around it like white feathers.

"How much did you get done today?" I asked, feeding him a piece of potato.

"Four pages," he said, chewing rapidly before the next cycle. "On the essay. The neck cramps were brutal by three o'clock, but the sentence was almost right. I couldn't leave it dangling."

I looked at the typed page currently in the carriage. It was covered in dark, dense text, typed one laborious key at a time. To write a single paragraph, Arthur had to lean his head forward, clamp the stick between his molars, and strike the keys using only the muscles of his jaw and neck. Hundreds of strikes per page. Thousands a day. His teeth were worn down, his jaw constantly bruised, yet his prose was exquisite—sharp, muscular, and devoid of a single wasted syllable.

"Four pages with a stick in your mouth," I said quietly. "Most writers I know spend four hours picking a font."

"They have too many limbs," Arthur snapped, though his eyes burned with pride. "Limbs are a distraction. You walk around, you make tea, you look out the window. Me? I have nowhere to go. The sentence is the only door out of this room."

He gestured with his eyes toward the stick. "Put it in. I want to fix the cadence on paragraph three before my jaw gives out."

I held the sanitized rubber grip to his mouth. He took it greedily, like a soldier reaching for a rifle. Immediately, the posture of his face changed. The humor evaporated, replaced by an terrifying, absolute focus. 

His head dipped. *Clack.* 
*Whoosh-click.* 
His head pivoted. *Clack.* 

The mechanical thud of the typewriter key merged with the mechanical heavy breathing of the iron lung. It was a strange, beautiful symphony—a man chained to a machine, using the machine's rhythm to forge something immortal. 

I sat back in the shadow of the yellow tank, watching his eyes dart across the mirror, watching his jaw work. In that dim room, amid the smell of stew and grease, I didn't see a helpless man. I saw a titan, wrestling God with a piece of plastic between his teeth, and winning.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe a severely disabled artist through the eyes of an admiring narrator who comes to study his inner strength and artistic discipline.
counterfactuals.output:
I came to Master Julian’s studio expecting to learn about color theory and light; I left having witnessed the purest manifestation of human willpower I will ever know.

To the uninitiated, Julian’s physical reality was daunting. Trapped in a body ruined by an aggressive, degenerative neurological disease, he possessed no movement below his chin, save for a slight, deliberate tilt of his neck. His breath was aided by a quiet, rhythmic hum of hydraulics, and his hands rested in his lap like folded paper, motionless and frail. 

Yet, the moment you entered his sun-drenched sanctuary, any illusion of fragility shattered. Julian did not inhabit that room as an invalid; he ruled it as a commander. 

His easel was a marvel of custom engineering—a colossal, motorized iron frame that lowered, raised, and rotated the canvas at the touch of a chin-operated joystick. Where other painters paced back and forth, stepping back to judge perspective, Julian commanded the canvas to bow to him. But the true miracle was his brushwork.

Holding a slender, carbon-fiber extension between his teeth, Julian painted with his jaw, his neck, and the unyielding core of his spirit. 

I spent months sitting in the corner of his loft, my own sketchbook resting limply in my lap, hypnotized by his process. Painting, for Julian, was not a casual act of self-expression; it was an athletic, sacred ritual that demanded total, uncompromising discipline. Because every stroke required immense physical exertion, he could not afford a single wasted movement. He had eliminated all trial and error from his hands and moved it entirely into his mind.

He would spend an hour in absolute stillness, staring at a six-foot canvas. His eyes—sharp, vivid, and brimming with incandescent intelligence—would track across the gessoed linen. He was calculating the exact weight of the paint, the precise angle of the stroke, the friction of the bristles, and the tension of his jaw muscles. 

When he finally leaned forward to strike, the air in the studio went taut. 

With painful, agonizing precision, he would guide the brush. A bead of sweat would roll down his temple; his breathing would quicken, clashing with the mechanical pulse of his respirator. His jaw muscles would cord and flex under the strain. Yet, the line he left on the canvas was never trembling. It was soaring, fluid, and impossibly delicate. 

Where I, with my two fully functioning hands, would rush and make careless marks, Julian worked with the terrifying focus of a master jeweler. A single passage of a sky might take him six hours of intense physical labor, leaving him drenched and trembling with exhaustion by dusk. But the resulting image was transcendent. There was no grief in his art, no self-pity, no mournful reflections on what he had lost. His canvases were violent explosions of light, complex architectural geometry, and vibrant, triumphant color. 

I remember asking him once, during a quiet afternoon while I mixed his oils, how he endured the sheer physical agony of a long painting session. 

He waited as I held the water straw to his lips. After drinking, he turned his sharp gaze onto me. He did not speak often—his voice was a low, raspy thread—but when he did, every word carried the weight of a stone.

"The body is just a vessel that resists," he whispered, his eyes locking onto mine with fierce clarity. "When you stop fighting the vessel, you find the space where the work actually lives. My canvas is not out there, student. It is in here. The stick is just a bridge."

In that moment, I understood the profound nature of his strength. Julian had not merely adapted to his disability; he had stripped away every distraction that plagues lesser artists. He had no room for laziness, no space for hesitation, no luxury of taking his medium for granted. His disability had burned away everything frivolous, leaving behind a distilled, terrifyingly pure artistic soul.

To study under Julian was to realize that true discipline is not about physical capability; it is an act of defiance. It is the refusal to let the quiet decay of the world dictate the boundaries of one's imagination. Every stroke of his brush was a triumph over physics, a battle won by sheer force of mind, and a reminder that the human spirit, when fully ignited, is entirely indomitable.
